versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 10 This is the account of Shem. Two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, he became the father of Arphaxad. 11 And after he had become the father of Arphaxad, Shem lived 500 years and had other sons and daughters.
12 When Arphaxad was 35 years old, he became the father of Shelah. 13 And after he had become the father of Shelah, Arphaxad lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.
14 When Shelah was 30 years old, he became the father of Eber. 15 And after he had become the father of Eber, Shelah lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.
16 When Eber was 34 years old, he became the father of Peleg. 17 And after he had become the father of Peleg, Eber lived 430 years and had other sons and daughters.
18 When Peleg was 30 years old, he became the father of Reu. 19 And after he had become the father of Reu, Peleg lived 209 years and had other sons and daughters.
20 When Reu was 32 years old, he became the father of Serug. 21 And after he had become the father of Serug, Reu lived 207 years and had other sons and daughters.
22 When Serug was 30 years old, he became the father of Nahor. 23 And after he had become the father of Nahor, Serug lived 200 years and had other sons and daughters.
24 When Nahor was 29 years old, he became the father of Terah. 25 And after he had become the father of Terah, Nahor lived 119 years and had other sons and daughters.
26 When Terah was 70 years old, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

context_lines: After the scattering at Babel, the account follows one branch of Noah's family. It begins with Shem, two years after the flood, and moves through Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, and Terah. Terah's three sons introduce Abram, who will become the central figure in the next part of Genesis.

Chapter 10 traced Eber's descendants through Joktan's many sons; this list takes the other branch, through Peleg. Its repeated pattern of a son's birth, further years, and other children resembles chapter 5. The listed lifespans generally become shorter as the account moves toward Abram, although the change is not an even decline from one generation to the next.

These verses supply names and ages, with few details about the people's lives. Their place in the family record does not establish that every person named was faithful to God. [Joshua 24:2–3](https://biblehub.com/bsb/joshua/24.htm) later says that Terah's household served other gods before describing God's call of Abraham.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand this genealogy as the bridge from Noah's family to Abraham, preparing for God's promises to him. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 11:10](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) emphasize the movement toward Abraham, and the [US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 11:10–26](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/11) likewise describes its place at this turning point in the book.
god_plan_lines: [Luke 3:34–36](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/3.htm) includes these ancestors as it traces Jesus' family back through Abraham, Shem, and Noah. A list that may first look like a pause in the story becomes part of the connection between the earliest generations and the coming of Christ.

There is a detail worth noticing when reading the two lists together: Luke names Cainan between Arphaxad and Shelah, while the Genesis text printed here does not. The [US Catholic bishops' note on Genesis 11:12](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/genesis/11) identifies that additional name in the Greek form of the genealogy. The difference belongs to the history of the texts; the shared line still connects Abraham with the earlier family through whom Luke traces Jesus.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
